speaker: Grace Liu
text: Welcome to Main Street Forum. Tonight we're with Dana Reyes, and the first question from the audience is about grocery prices.

speaker: Dana Reyes
text: Families here are paying more for everything at the checkout line, and I don't think Washington has been honest about why.

speaker: Dana Reyes
text: On trade, I want targeted tariffs on countries that dump steel below cost, not a tax on every pair of sneakers a family buys.

speaker: Dana Reyes
text: Childcare costs more than rent for a lot of young parents in this district, and that should embarrass all of us.

speaker: Grace Liu
text: Ms. Reyes, your opponent says your trade plan is soft. How do you respond?

speaker: Dana Reyes
text: Soft is pretending a tariff on everything is free. Somebody pays it, and it's usually the person buying school supplies.

episode_title: Reyes on the cost of living
speaker: Ellen Cho
text: Dana Reyes is back on The Morning Ledger. We're talking cost of living today.

episode_title: Reyes on the cost of living
speaker: Dana Reyes
text: I'd cap what families pay for childcare at seven percent of income, and I'd pay for it by closing the carried interest loophole.

episode_title: Reyes on the cost of living
speaker: Dana Reyes
text: Housing is the other half of this. You can't tell people to work harder when the rent goes up faster than the paycheck.

speaker: Tom Reiner
text: Marcus Whitfield is campaigning on jobs and automation. Here's what he told a crowd in Dayton.

speaker: Marcus Whitfield
text: If a company replaces a thousand workers with software, it should pay into the same retraining fund those workers paid into.

speaker: Marcus Whitfield
text: I support a fifteen-dollar minimum wage indexed to inflation, and I'm not going to apologize for that.

speaker: Tom Reiner
text: Critics say Whitfield's retraining fund would cost billions and slow down hiring.

episode_title: Dana Reyes on trade and tariffs
speaker: Ellen Cho
text: Today on The Morning Ledger, Dana Reyes on trade. Let's start with tariffs.

episode_title: Dana Reyes on trade and tariffs
speaker: Dana Reyes
text: A blanket tariff is a sales tax with a flag on it. I'm for tariffs that punish cheating, not tariffs that punish shoppers.

episode_title: Dana Reyes on trade and tariffs
speaker: Dana Reyes
text: If we're going to put a tariff on steel, the revenue should go straight back into the towns that lost their mills.

episode_title: Dana Reyes on trade and tariffs
speaker: Ellen Cho
text: Some economists say even targeted tariffs raise prices. Is that a risk you're willing to take?

episode_title: Dana Reyes on trade and tariffs
speaker: Dana Reyes
text: Every policy has a cost. The question is whether the cost lands on the company that broke the rules or on the family at the register.

episode_title: Dana Reyes on trade and tariffs
speaker: Dana Reyes
text: I'm not going to promise you lower prices by Christmas. I'm going to promise you a trade policy that doesn't lie to you.

speaker: Lena Marsh
text: Tariffs are dominating the race today. Dana Reyes went on a podcast this morning, and Marcus Whitfield fired back.

speaker: Marcus Whitfield
text: Tariffs on steel and aluminum brought jobs back to Ohio. My opponent wants to talk about sneakers; I want to talk about paychecks.

speaker: Lena Marsh
text: Reyes basically said a blanket tariff is just a tax on shoppers, and her campaign says the line was about fairness.

speaker: Marcus Whitfield
text: I'd put a ten percent tariff on any company that moves a factory overseas and then sells the product back here.

speaker: Sam Ortiz
text: This week the tariff debate got loud. Let's break down what each candidate actually proposed.

speaker: Sam Ortiz
text: Reyes says she wants tariffs that punish cheating. Whitfield wants a ten percent tariff on companies that offshore. Anand hasn't said much about tariffs at all.

speaker: Sam Ortiz
text: Economists we talked to say a broad tariff usually shows up in consumer prices within a year.

speaker: Ray Okafor
text: Marcus Whitfield, welcome to Statehouse Hour. You've been talking a lot about AI.

speaker: Marcus Whitfield
text: AI is going to be the biggest jobs story of the decade, and right now nobody in this race has a plan for the people it displaces.

speaker: Marcus Whitfield
text: I'd require any company over five hundred employees to give ninety days' notice before automating a job away.

speaker: Ray Okafor
text: What about the minimum wage? You've said fifteen dollars before.

speaker: Marcus Whitfield
text: Fifteen, indexed to inflation, phased in over three years for small businesses.

speaker: Mia Torres
text: Fact check time. Whitfield says steel tariffs brought jobs back to Ohio. Let's look at the numbers.

speaker: Mia Torres
text: Steel employment in Ohio rose about two percent after the tariffs, but most of that was in plants that were already reopening. Verdict: partly true.

speaker: Jules Park
text: Marcus Whitfield said something at a rally yesterday that's all over my feed. Here it is.

speaker: Marcus Whitfield
text: Robots don't pay rent, and they don't pay payroll tax either. So who's going to fund Social Security when the jobs are gone?

speaker: Jules Park
text: Love it or hate it, that line has two million views.

speaker: Jules Park
text: A lot of you asked what Whitfield actually wants to do about AI. It's a notice rule and a retraining fund, not a robot tax.

speaker: Jules Park
text: Some of you said he wants to ban AI. He doesn't. He said he wants ninety days' notice before a job is automated.

speaker: Lena Marsh
text: AI and jobs is now a top issue in polling, and the candidates are scrambling to respond.

speaker: Priya Anand
text: I'm less worried about robots than about rent. You can retrain for a new job, but you can't retrain your way out of a housing shortage.

speaker: Dana Reyes
text: AI should make work better, not disposable. I'd start by making sure the companies that profit from it also pay into worker training.

speaker: Grace Liu
text: Our guest tonight is Priya Anand. Let's start with housing.

speaker: Priya Anand
text: We should be building starter homes, not just studios. A family can't raise kids in four hundred square feet.

speaker: Priya Anand
text: I'd cap insulin at thirty-five dollars a month for everyone, not just people on Medicare.

speaker: Priya Anand
text: Wildfire insurance is becoming impossible to buy in half this state. That's a climate problem and a housing problem at the same time.

speaker: Grace Liu
text: Ms. Anand, where do you stand on tariffs?

speaker: Priya Anand
text: I'd rather talk about what we build here than about what we block at the border.

speaker: Ellen Cho
text: Priya Anand joins us to talk about her housing plan.

speaker: Priya Anand
text: My plan legalizes duplexes and townhomes near every transit stop and cuts permit times to sixty days.

speaker: Priya Anand
text: If we don't build, rents keep climbing. There is no version of this where doing nothing is free.

speaker: Mia Torres
text: Anand says her plan cuts permit times to sixty days. Is that realistic?

speaker: Mia Torres
text: Two nearby cities already hit sixty days after similar reforms, so the claim is plausible. Verdict: mostly true.

speaker: Lena Marsh
text: Last night's debate got heated on housing and trade. Here are the moments people are talking about.

speaker: Priya Anand
text: My opponents keep fighting about tariffs while your rent goes up every single year.

speaker: Marcus Whitfield
text: Ms. Anand, you can't build houses without steel, and you can't buy steel without a job.

speaker: Dana Reyes
text: I agree with Priya on housing and I agree with Marcus on steel. I just don't agree with taxing families to prove a point.

speaker: Sam Ortiz
text: Wildfire insurance is collapsing in parts of the West. Here's what the candidates have said.

speaker: Sam Ortiz
text: Anand has called it a climate problem and a housing problem. Reyes and Whitfield haven't released plans yet.

speaker: Ray Okafor
text: Dana Reyes, you've made childcare a centerpiece of this campaign.

speaker: Dana Reyes
text: No family should pay more than seven percent of its income for childcare. That's the whole plan in one sentence.

speaker: Dana Reyes
text: Childcare workers should earn enough to afford childcare themselves. Right now a lot of them can't.

speaker: Tom Reiner
text: Insulin prices are back in the headlines, and one candidate has made them central.

speaker: Priya Anand
text: Thirty-five dollars a month. That's what insulin should cost, whether you're sixty-five or twenty-five.

speaker: Tom Reiner
text: Whitfield's campaign says he also supports an insulin cap, but he hasn't said what the cap would be.
